Functor.Liftr.code: Functor.Liftr.{u} {F : Type u → Type u} [Functor F] {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) (x y : F α) : Prop
Functor.Liftr.comment:
If we consider `x : F α` to, in some sense, contain values of type `α`, then
`Liftr r x y` relates `x` and `y` iff (1) `x` and `y` have the same shape and
(2) we can pair values `a` from `x` and `b` from `y` so that `r a b` holds.

explanatories.Prod.fst: The first element of a pair.
explanatories.Prod.snd: The second element of a pair.

Functor.Liftr.fullDefinition: def Liftr {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) (x y : F α) : Prop :=   ∃ u : F { p : α × α // r p.fst p.snd },     (fun t : { p : α × α // r p.fst p.snd } => t.val.fst) <$> u = x ∧       (fun t : { p : α × α // r p.fst p.snd } => t.val.snd) <$> u = y
Functor.Liftr.description: This definition establishes a relation between two functorial values of the same type based on a given property, asserting that they are related if they have equivalent structure and their constituent values satisfy the specified property.

Functor.Liftp.comment:
If we consider `x : F α` to, in some sense, contain values of type `α`,
predicate `Liftp p x` holds iff every value contained by `x` satisfies `p`.

explanatories.Subtype.val: The value of a subtype is the underlying element of the type that satisfies a given property.

Functor.Liftp.fullDefinition: def Liftp {α : Type u} (p : α → Prop) (x : F α) : Prop :=   ∃ u : F (Subtype p), Subtype.val <$> u = x
Functor.Liftp.description: This definition establishes a condition for a functor that relates to whether all values encapsulated within it satisfy a specified property.

Functor.Liftr.code: Functor.Liftr.{u} {F : Type u → Type u} [Functor F] {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) (x y : F α) : Prop
Functor.Liftr.comment:
If we consider `x : F α` to, in some sense, contain values of type `α`, then
`Liftr r x y` relates `x` and `y` iff (1) `x` and `y` have the same shape and
(2) we can pair values `a` from `x` and `b` from `y` so that `r a b` holds.

explanatories.Prod.fst: The first element of a pair.
explanatories.Prod.snd: The second element of a pair.

Functor.Liftr.fullDefinition: def Liftr {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) (x y : F α) : Prop :=   ∃ u : F { p : α × α // r p.fst p.snd },     (fun t : { p : α × α // r p.fst p.snd } => t.val.fst) <$> u = x ∧       (fun t : { p : α × α // r p.fst p.snd } => t.val.snd) <$> u = y
Functor.Liftr.description: This definition establishes a relation between two functorial values of the same type based on a given property, asserting that they are related if they have equivalent structure and their constituent values satisfy the specified property.

Functor.supp.fullDefinition: def supp {α : Type u} (x : F α) : Set α :=   { y : α | ∀ ⦃p⦄, Liftp p x → p y }

Functor.mapConstRev.code: Functor.mapConstRev.{u, v} {f : Type u → Type v} [Functor f] {α β : Type u} : f β → α → f α
Functor.mapConstRev.comment:
If `f` is a functor, if `fb : f β` and `a : α`, then `mapConstRev fb a` is the result of
applying `f.map` to the constant function `β → α` sending everything to `a`, and then
evaluating at `fb`. In other words it's `const a <$> fb`.

explanatories.Functor.Const: The constant functor maps every type to a fixed type, allowing for the construction of structures that depend solely on that fixed value.

Functor.mapConstRev.fullDefinition: abbrev mapConstRev {f : Type u → Type v} [Functor f] {α β : Type u} :     f β → α → f α :=   fun a b => Functor.mapConst b a
Functor.mapConstRev.description: This definition describes a function that applies a functor to a constant function which maps all elements to a specified value, effectively transforming a functor containing one type into a functor containing another.

WriterT.monad.comment:
Creates an instance of Monad, with an explicitly given empty and append operation.

Previously, this would have used an instance of `[Monoid ω]` as input.
In practice, however, WriterT is used for logging and creating lists so restricting to

This is used to derive instances for both `[EmptyCollection ω] [Append ω]` and `[Monoid ω]`.

Monoid.Foldl.comment:
For a list, foldl f x [y₀,y₁] reduces as follows:

```
calc  foldl f x [y₀,y₁]
    = foldl f (f x y₀) [y₁]      : rfl
... = foldl f (f (f x y₀) y₁) [] : rfl
... = f (f x y₀) y₁              : rfl
```
with
```
f : α → β → α
x : α
[y₀,y₁] : List β
```

We can view the above as a composition of functions:
```
... = f (f x y₀) y₁              : rfl
... = flip f y₁ (flip f y₀ x)    : rfl
... = (flip f y₁ ∘ flip f y₀) x  : rfl
```

We can use traverse and const to construct this composition:
```
calc   const.run (traverse (fun y ↦ const.mk' (flip f y)) [y₀,y₁]) x
     = const.run ((::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₀) <*>
         traverse (fun y ↦ const.mk' (flip f y)) [y₁]) x
...  = const.run ((::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₀) <*>
         ( (::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₁) <*> traverse (fun y ↦ const.mk' (flip f y)) [] )) x
...  = const.run ((::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₀) <*>
         ( (::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₁) <*> pure [] )) x
...  = const.run ( ((::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₁) <*> pure []) ∘
         ((::) <$> const.mk' (flip f y₀)) ) x
...  = const.run ( const.mk' (flip f y₁) ∘ const.mk' (flip f y₀) ) x
...  = const.run ( flip f y₁ ∘ flip f y₀ ) x
...  = f (f x y₀) y₁
```

And this is how `const` turns a monoid into an applicative functor and
how the monoid of endofunctions define `Foldl`.

Traversable.toList.code: Traversable.toList.{u} {α : Type u} {t : Type u → Type u} [Traversable t] : t α → List α
Traversable.toList.comment:
Conceptually, `toList` collects all the elements of a collection
in a list. This idea is formalized by

  `lemma toList_spec (x : t α) : toList x = foldMap FreeMonoid.mk x`.

The definition of `toList` is based on `foldl` and `List.cons` for
speed. It is faster than using `foldMap FreeMonoid.mk` because, by
using `foldl` and `List.cons`, each insertion is done in constant
time. As a consequence, `toList` performs in linear.

On the other hand, `foldMap FreeMonoid.mk` creates a singleton list
around each element and concatenates all the resulting lists. In
`xs ++ ys`, concatenation takes a time proportional to `length xs`. Since
the order in which concatenation is evaluated is unspecified, nothing
prevents each element of the traversable to be appended at the end
`xs ++ [x]` which would yield a `O(n²)` run time.
